_note: The Gym manifest (WP25a): which grammar points act as selectable form categories, grouped into picker columns. 'point' must match the grammar point title exactly (resolved to ids at request time). 'usage' is the plain-language hover explanation; 'example' is a real drill sentence from that point. 'nonstandard': entries hidden behind the 'include non-standard words' toggle.

entries.label: Ne / ce
entries.usage: Use it to say what someone or something is: end with ne after a man, a plural, or a masculine word, and ce after a woman or a feminine word like mota.
entries.example: Ni malami ne. — I am a (male) teacher.

entries.label: Completive (na, ya)
entries.usage: Use it for something already done: na ci (I ate), sun tafi (they left).
entries.example: Na ci abinci. — I ate food.

entries.label: Continuous (ina, yana)
entries.usage: Use it for what is going on right now: ina, kana, yana and the -ing shape of the verb.
entries.example: Ina cin abinci. — I am eating food.

entries.label: Future (zan)
entries.usage: Use it for what has not happened yet: zan tafi (I will go), za ta dawo (she will come back).
entries.example: Zan tafi gida. — I will go home.

entries.label: Habitual (nakan)
entries.usage: Use it for what someone does again and again, with words like kullum or kowace rana.
entries.example: Nakan sha shayi da safe. — I usually drink tea in the morning.

entries.label: Subjunctive (ka zo)
entries.usage: Use these short pronouns after wanting, letting or telling someone to do something: ina so ka zo, bari mu je.
entries.example: Ina so ka zo. — I want you to come.

entries.label: Commands & kada
entries.usage: Use the bare verb to tell someone to do something (Zo!) and kada plus the short pronoun to tell them not to (Kada ka tafi!).
entries.example: Zo nan! — Come here!

entries.label: Relative suka/aka
entries.usage: After da (who, that) and in it-was sentences, sun becomes suka, mun becomes muka, an becomes aka.
entries.example: Mutanen da suka zo jiya sun tafi. — The people who came yesterday have left.

entries.label: Relative -ke
entries.usage: In who/that clauses and straight after a question word, yana becomes yake and kana becomes kake.
entries.example: Ina kake zaune? — Where do you live? (you-m)

entries.label: Impersonal an/ana
entries.usage: Use an or ana when it does not matter who did it: An gina gida (a house was built).
entries.example: An gina sabon gida. — A new house has been built.

entries.point: Verbal nouns in the continuous (cin, shan, zuwa)
entries.label: Verbal nouns
entries.usage: After ina, yana and the rest the verb changes shape before its object: ci becomes cin, sha becomes shan, zo becomes zuwa.
entries.example: Ina cin abinci. — I am eating food.

entries.label: Verb grades
entries.usage: Use the -ar form when the action is aimed at someone else (saya buy becomes sayar da sell) and the -u form when something simply gets done to a thing (dafa cook becomes dafu be cooked).
entries.example: Ya sayar da tsohuwar motarsa. — He sold his old car.

entries.point: Choosing the aspect — jiya, yanzu, kowace rana
entries.label: Which aspect?
entries.usage: Let the time word pick the pronoun for you: jiya takes na, yanzu takes ina, kullum takes nakan, gobe takes zan.
entries.example: Jiya na tafi kasuwa. — Yesterday I went to the market.

entries.point: To have: da (ina da, ba ni da)
entries.label: Have (da)
entries.usage: Use ina da, yana da to say you have something, and ba ni da, ba shi da to say you have not.
entries.example: Ina da mota. — I have a car.

entries.label: Independent pronouns
entries.usage: Use these standalone words for I, you, he and the rest — and say kai to a man, ke to a woman.
entries.example: Ni malami ne. — I am a teacher.

entries.label: Object pronouns
entries.usage: Use these straight after the verb for the person or thing it happens to: Na gan shi (I saw him).
entries.example: Na gan shi a kasuwa. — I saw him at the market.

entries.label: Indirect objects
entries.usage: Use mini, maka, masa right after the verb for the person you do something to or for.
entries.example: Ya rubuta mini wasiƙa. — He wrote me a letter.

entries.label: Possessives (-na)
entries.usage: Stick the owner on the end of the thing owned: littafina (my book), motarsa (his car).
entries.example: Littafina yana nan. — My book is here.

entries.label: Linker -n/-r
entries.usage: Use it to say whose something is: add -n to the first noun (littafin Audu) or -r if that noun is a feminine one like mota (motar Audu).
entries.example: Littafin Audu yana nan. — Audu's book is here.

entries.label: Plurals
entries.usage: Use it when you mean more than one — the word itself changes shape: mota becomes motoci, gida becomes gidaje.
entries.example: Ina da motoci biyu. — I have two cars.

entries.label: This / that
entries.usage: Point something out with wannan (this), wancan or waccan (that), waɗannan (these) — they go in front of the noun.
entries.example: Wannan littafi nawa ne. — This book is mine.

entries.label: Mai / masu
entries.usage: Use mai plus a noun to describe something (gida mai kyau, a fine house), masu when there is more than one.
entries.example: Wannan gida mai kyau ne. — This is a beautiful house.

entries.point: Numbers after the noun (biyu, goma, nawa)
entries.label: Numbers & nawa
entries.usage: Put the number after the noun, not before it — mota biyu (two cars) — and use nawa in the same spot to ask how many.
entries.example: Ina da yara biyu. — I have two children.

entries.label: Ɗan-compounds
entries.usage: Put ɗan (ʼyar for a woman, ʼyan for several) in front of a noun to say where someone belongs or what they do: ɗan kasuwa, a trader.
entries.example: Shi ɗan Nijeriya ne. — He is a Nigerian.

entries.label: Akwai / babu
entries.usage: Say there is with akwai and there is no with babu.
entries.example: Akwai ruwa a gida. — There is water at home.

entries.label: Negation (ba…ba)
entries.usage: Say something did not happen by wrapping the whole sentence in ba … ba: Ban ci ba (I didn't eat).
entries.example: Ban ci abinci ba. — I did not eat food.

entries.label: Question words
entries.usage: Ask with me (what), wa (who), ina (where) and yaushe (when) at the front of the sentence, and use nawa (how much/how many) after the noun you are counting: littattafai nawa?
entries.example: Me ka ci? — What did you eat?

entries.label: Relative clauses
entries.usage: Say more about a person or thing with da, or with wanda, wadda, waɗanda: the man who came, the car that I bought.
entries.example: Mutumin da ya zo malami ne. — The man who came is a teacher.

entries.label: Focus fronting
entries.usage: Put the word you want to stress first and follow it with ne or ce to mean it was THAT one: Audu ne ya zo.
entries.example: Audu ne ya zo. — It was Audu who came.

entries.label: If (idan)
entries.usage: Set up a condition with idan or its short form in: Idan ka zo, za mu ci abinci.
entries.example: Idan ka zo, za mu ci abinci. — If you come, we will eat.

entries.label: Comparison (fi)
entries.usage: Say one thing beats another with fi: Ya fi ni tsayi (he is taller than me).
entries.example: Ya fi ni tsayi. — He is taller than me.

entries.point: Because and in order to: don, domin, saboda
entries.label: Because / purpose
entries.usage: Give the reason with saboda or domin, and the purpose with don plus a short pronoun: na zo don in gan ka.
entries.example: Na zo don in gan ka. — I came in order to see you.

entries.label: Before / after
entries.usage: Line two events up in time: kafin ka tafi (before you go), bayan ya gama (after he finished).
entries.example: Kafin ka tafi, kashe wuta. — Before you go, turn off the light.

entries.label: Kuma, amma, har
entries.usage: Stitch sentences together: kuma adds, amma turns, har stretches, ma tags something on.
entries.example: Ya sayi gurasa kuma ya sayi madara. — He bought bread and also bought milk.

entries.label: Sai
entries.usage: One small word for until, then, only and except: sai gobe (see you tomorrow), kowa ya tafi sai Audu (everyone left except Audu).
entries.example: Sai gobe! — See you tomorrow!

entries.label: Ko (or, any-)
entries.usage: Ko offers a choice (shayi ko kofi), says whether, checks back (ko ba haka ba?) and builds kowa (everyone) and komai (everything).
entries.example: Kana son shayi ko kofi? — Do you want tea or coffee?

entries.label: Reported speech
entries.usage: Use cewa to pass on what somebody said, heard or is sure of: Ya ce cewa zai zo.
entries.example: Ya ce cewa zai zo. — He said that he would come.

entries.label: Reduplication
entries.usage: Double a word to spread it out or soften it: biyu-biyu (two by two), daban-daban (all sorts), ja-ja (reddish).
entries.example: Sun shiga biyu-biyu. — They entered two by two.

entries.label: Intensifiers (fat, wur)
entries.usage: Each quality has its own booster word that goes with nothing else: fari fat (snow-white), ja wur (blazing red), shiru tsit (dead silent).
entries.example: Rigarsa fara ce fat. — His gown is snow-white.

entries.label: Particles (fa, dai)
entries.usage: The small words that set the tone: fa turns it back on the listener, mana urges, dai softens, ashe means so that's how it is.
entries.example: Kai fa, yaya aikinka? — And you, how is your work?

entries.label: Greetings
entries.usage: Use the greeting the moment calls for: barka da safiya early in the day, gafara dai to announce yourself, ranka ya daɗe to an elder or a chief.
entries.example: 'Ranka ya daɗe!' ya gaishe sarki. — 'May your life be long!' he greeted the emir.

entries.label: Proverbs
entries.usage: Drop one of these fixed sayings to settle a point the way an elder would.
entries.example: Sannu ba ta hana zuwa. — Going slowly does not prevent arriving.
